A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Open Proof Corpus study. Their main text, figures, tables, equations and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and added analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original human annotations, proof-generation and judging evaluations, best-of-n experiments, and results for an 8B model fine-tuned on the corpus.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds undergraduate judging evaluations, reference-solution controls, and analyses of difficulty, problem category and potential contamination.

M1.justification: The corpus-construction pipeline, GRPO-trained 8B judge and four best-of-n procedures remain unchanged. The original generation, grading and selection prompts match across v1 Appendix E and v2 Appendix I. The added reference-solution prompt supports a diagnostic experiment rather than a revision of the core method.

E1.justification: The corpus remains 5,062 proofs across 1,010 problems, with the same competition sources. v2 adds explicit undergraduate out-of-distribution judging and judging with supplied official solutions, extending the evaluated population and input conditions within the existing mathematical domain.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds GPT-5 and Grok-4 while removing Qwen3-30B-A3B and the length-based/random baseline. Section 5.3 replaces DeepSeek-Prover-V2 with Goedel-Prover-V2 as the formal comparator. These changes update both central comparison sets; Seed-Prover is discussed separately and explicitly excluded from direct comparison.

E3.justification: v1 describes the larger best-of-n evaluation as covering the entire subset; v2 specifies 134 problems and discloses 18 exclusions caused by a Swiss-selection bug. v2 also introduces a 560-proof undergraduate judging protocol and a with/without-reference-solution control. Newly supplied training hyperparameters document the existing experiment rather than establishing changed training.

E4.justification: v2 adds undergraduate generalization testing, a reference-solution contamination stress test, difficulty/category breakdowns, and standard-versus-nonstandard competition analysis (Section 5.6 and Appendix C). These substantially expand robustness and diagnostic evidence. The original self-evaluation analysis and qualitative error cases remain, with the latter relocated from Appendix C to E.

E5.justification: v1's main performance plots and judge tables report point estimates without confidence intervals. v2 adds error bars to existing plots and 95% intervals for aggregate and prover-specific judging results in Tables 7–8, specifying the large-sample normal approximation. The PDFs do not establish an increase in repeated runs or seeds.

E6.justification: v2 adds GPT-5 results of 89.3% pass@1 and 90.8% maj@5, making it the reported leading judge, plus substantial new robustness results. The undergraduate test reports 77.0% maj@5 for OPC-R1-8B versus 72.4% for its base model. Its original 88.1% result remains unchanged. The larger-set discrete-selection value changes from 31.4% to 31.5% alongside the revised subset description, not an established same-setting gain.

T1.justification: The Bradley–Terry probability equation and fitting procedure, independent-judge noise calculation, and ranking-complexity statements remain unchanged. No new theorem, proof or substantive mathematical derivation is introduced.

C1.justification: The corpus contribution and central research questions remain. v2 narrows the trained judge's standing from matching the best model to matching Gemini and approaching GPT-5. The headline informal/formal advantage changes from 11 times to 4 times with the updated comparator, and the best judge is now described as matching human performance.

C2.justification: v1's general contamination caveat and untested generalization warning become detailed, experiment-specific interpretations. v2 argues that contamination has limited impact while acknowledging it cannot be excluded, interprets undergraduate results as evidence of transfer, distinguishes agentic formal systems, and notes that GPT-5 and Grok-4 were evaluated only as judges. These materially expand applicability boundaries and qualifications.

D1.justification: New Appendix D specifies 1,733 training proofs, VERL, learning rate 10^-6, 14,000-token responses, 10 rollouts and batch size 16, alongside evaluation defaults. v2 also expands annotation-process documentation and discloses undergraduate training exclusion. Access instructions change from direct project, dataset and interface URLs to supplementary-material references, with explicit SMT release restrictions; actual external availability cannot be verified from the PDFs.

R1.justification: Section 2 refocuses the general LLM-judge discussion on mathematical and educational grading, adding Chevalier et al. and Zhao et al. References also expand to Goedel-Prover-V2, Seed-Prover, contamination and the training framework, while several benchmark and self-correction references disappear. The broad positioning of OPC as a human-evaluated proof corpus remains.

P1.justification: The main narrative sequence and much retained prose remain recognizable. v2 revises the abstract and conclusion, expands explanations of the annotation process, adds Setup/Results-style signposts, and moves Future Work to Appendix F. Original prompts and qualitative examples are largely retained.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to a predominantly single-column layout, with redesigned headings and table placement. v1 Figures 6–7 become panels of v2 Figure 6; Table 3 is transposed without changing matched results. New analysis figures and tables, error bars, revised axes and updated overview graphics substantially change the presentation.

improvement.justification: v1 supported its trained-judge contribution with sparse training details, point estimates and no out-of-distribution test. v2 addresses these important gaps through explicit training settings, confidence intervals and a 560-proof undergraduate evaluation showing a smaller retained advantage over the base model (77.0% versus 72.4% maj@5). These additions substantially strengthen reproducibility and evidential assessment. Contamination remains unresolved and direct resource links are removed, but these limitations do not outweigh the gains.
